headline: New Mexico sues Justice Department for unredacted Epstein Library records
standfirst: The complaint names Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and is pleaded under the Administrative Procedure Act, not FOIA.

paragraphs.text: New Mexico has sued the Justice Department and Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia over withheld Epstein records. The case is docketed as No. 1:26-cv-02762-AHA and assigned to Judge Amir H. Ali. It is pleaded as review of agency action under the Administrative Procedure Act rather than as a FOIA case. The state seeks the redacted materials in the federal 'Epstein Library', compiled under Section 2(a)(1)-(9) of the Epstein Files Transparency Act, Public Law 119-38 (19 November 2025).

New Mexico states it is investigating potential felony offences including homicide, kidnapping, criminal sexual penetration, criminal sexual contact and human trafficking, under named provisions of the New Mexico criminal code. It reopened its criminal investigation on 19 February 2026, after the Justice Department's January 2026 release of the Epstein files. The filing states the released files contain more than 13,000 references to Zorro Ranch and more than 5,000 references to New Mexico as locations where victims were trafficked, groomed and assaulted.

On 1 April 2026, an Associate Deputy Attorney General affirmed the department's commitment to assisting and requested that New Mexico submit a Touhy letter through standard channels. New Mexico's Touhy letter of 3 May 2026 requested a response by 11 May 2026. The suit was filed on 5 August 2026, 86 days after that date passed.

The federal district office's response, dated 30 June 2026 and delivered on 14 July, stated it had neither collected nor retained investigative materials. The thirty-one accompanying pages consisted largely of a public news article, a public press release by a former governor, correspondence New Mexico had itself sent, and a list of follow-up questions.

Asked whether the federal government would join New Mexico in seeking a modification of the protective orders it cited as the obstacle, so that the orders would expressly permit disclosure for law-enforcement purposes, a Deputy United States Attorney responded that such cooperation was 'unlikely'. That official identified no path through which the two offices could work together.

The complaint alleges federal officials made public assurances of cooperation during the same period the requests went unanswered. It cites a First Assistant United States Attorney who said on 12 June 2026, 'I anticipate full cooperation', and a department spokesperson who said on 7 July 2026 that the department 'stands ready to provide necessary assistance'.

The complaint dates the federal stand-down request to a telephone call on 23 July 2019 and cites a federal record of that call in the publicly released Epstein Files. New Mexico alleges federal prosecutors asked the state to stand down from its Zorro Ranch sex-trafficking investigation in July 2019, promising to refer state crimes back and share information once the federal work concluded. The stated federal rationale for the request was avoiding the risk that parallel investigations would produce inconsistent statements exploitable by defence counsel. Jeffrey Epstein died in federal custody on 10 August 2019, ending the federal prosecution.

New Mexico gave the federal government its entire investigative file — police reports, recorded witness interviews and materials on Epstein's use of state public lands — on 17 September 2019, after agreeing to stand down. Then-Attorney General Hector Balderas asked the federal government on 15 October 2019 to begin seizing Epstein's New Mexico land holdings for the benefit of survivors. New Mexico alleges the promised federal evidence was never provided.

The complaint states that federal law enforcement never searched Zorro Ranch. It cites a federal email of 23 August 2019, thirteen days after Epstein's death, that acknowledged a victim who may have been raped at the New Mexico residence while asserting there was no probable cause to search it.

The state's own formal request dates its search of the property to 9 March 2026. Investigators reported recovering evidence of prior excavation and altered substrate at the property inconsistent with the original construction timeline. State and county officials ordered construction at the property paused, alleging the owners failed to obtain required permits.

Zorro Ranch, roughly 8,000 acres in Santa Fe County, was sold at public auction in 2023 to San Rafael Ranch LLC, an entity registered with the New Mexico Secretary of State roughly one month before the purchase. The LLC's ownership was not disclosed at purchase and became public only after a street-name change and a contested property-tax assessment prompted public-records requests. The owner is Don Huffines, a former Texas state senator now running for Texas Comptroller; his wife Mary Catherine is listed as a trustee and his son Colin as an LLC manager. The owners intend to convert the property into a Christian retreat.

changed.to: Touhy request 3 May 2026; treated as denied 31 Jul 2026
